india-aff056b1e1.headline: Apple Pay may launch in India in October without UPI support
india-aff056b1e1.fulltext:
e-commerce
Apple Pay may launch in India in October without UPI support
Apple could begin with tokenised Visa and Mastercard payments as UPI talks continue
MUMBAI: Apple may be ready to make a payment play in India, but it could initially leave the country’s biggest payment button untouched. The company is reportedly considering launching Apple Pay in India as early as October, but without UPI support in the first phase, according to a Times of India report citing people familiar with the plans.
The reported launch would initially allow iPhone and Apple Watch users to make contactless payments at compatible point-of-sale terminals using tokenised Visa and Mastercard cards. Apple is understood to have held discussions with HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Axis Bank on provisioning cards for the service.
Apple has not officially confirmed an October launch, so the reported timeline and feature set could still change.
The bigger question is what happens to UPI. While Apple Pay’s card-first approach could get the service off the ground, leaving out UPI would mean missing the payment method that has become central to India’s digital transactions.
Apple is reportedly continuing discussions with the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) on integrating UPI into Apple Pay. One of the issues is authentication. Apple Pay typically relies on Face ID or Touch ID, while UPI transactions operate within India’s existing authentication and payment framework.
There is also a commercial wrinkle. India’s payments market works differently from several international markets, particularly because UPI transactions do not offer the same transaction economics associated with card payments. Apple would therefore have to navigate not just technical integration, but also local payment economics, banking relationships and regulatory requirements.
A card-led launch could nevertheless give Apple a foothold among its existing premium customer base while UPI discussions continue. Apple reportedly sold around 14 million iPhones in India in 2025, giving the company a sizeable installed base even though its overall smartphone market share remains relatively small.
For banks and card networks, Apple’s premium-heavy user base could make the ecosystem attractive, particularly among iPhone and Apple Watch owners who are already accustomed to contactless payments.
The timing could also dovetail with Apple’s annual iPhone cycle, potentially allowing the company to introduce its payment service alongside its next wave of devices.
But India is hardly short of digital payment options. Consumers already have deeply established UPI habits, making Apple’s challenge less about introducing contactless payments and more about persuading users to add another payment layer to an ecosystem they already navigate with ease.
If the reported timeline holds, Apple Pay could therefore enter India in stages cards first, UPI later. For now, however, the October launch remains unconfirmed.

world-847a3f7d97.fulltext:
Hello, and welcome back to This Is India.
For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?
Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”.
The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty, which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began.
Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added.
By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including:
 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons
  564,970 parts of explosive ordnance
  298 components of military vehicles
Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.)
An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes.
Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam.
Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay, writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”.
The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war.
Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel, and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back: “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.”
The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations.
The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party. The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court, demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive.
“In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern.
Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers, in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023.
India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests.

Three districts in particular – Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat – have been hit hard. other-interests-ae8470f747.headline: The proton is more quantum than we thought
other-interests-ae8470f747.fulltext:
Protons have more quantum innards than we previously knew, transforming our view of these particles that sit at the heart of every atom.
Researchers have long known that protons are made up of smaller particles called quarks and gluons, but the details of their behaviour and distribution have been challenging to pin down. Yet these details really matter – how well we understand the proton’s insides affects how well we can interpret experiments in which they are smashed, which aim to search for new particles or uncover the secrets of fundamental forces.
Physicists’ current best mathematical tool for understanding the proton’s insides is the parton model. This allows them to calculate the density of particles inside the proton probabilistically, pinpointing what its make-up is most likely to be like in accelerator experiments, for instance.
Advertisement
“The parton model is extremely powerful: it’s the main source of all our knowledge about the internal structure of the proton. But if you look at the modern state of it, you realise the picture behind it is pretty classical,” says Alexey Vladimirov at the Complutense University of Madrid. “This is, of course, false because we know quantum mechanics exists.”
Researchers have theorised about and looked for quantum effects within protons since the 1980s, says Vladimirov, but over the years, different experiments led to unclear and, at times, contradictory conclusions.
To get a clearer picture, he and his colleagues zeroed in on one process that quarks and gluons could be undergoing that is a hallmark of quantumness: interference. Quantum particles have a wave-like nature and interference is equivalent to two quantum matter waves overlapping and amplifying each other in some places, but cancelling each other out in others. Mathematically, where classically two probabilities would simply add, when there is interference, combining them produces more mathematical terms than just a sum.
The researchers devised a way to extract mathematical signatures of quantum interference from a combination of more than a dozen very varied datasets. For example, some data came from the CERN particle physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland, while some was collected at German national laboratory DESY across rather different kinds of experiments, none of which was designed to look for interference.
“All previous investigations failed because people tried to look at just one source [of data],” says Vladimirov. While it was a big technical challenge to put all the data together, it paid off in new clarity. The researchers could identify specific instances of quantum interference within a proton, such as a gluon interfering with a combination of a quark and an antiquark, which is its antimatter companion.
Vladimirov says this underlines how physicists ought to be more keenly aware of the proton’s quantumness. “It’s commonly accepted that the proton is almost like a classical bag of particles, and the fact that we demonstrate that it is not so means that it’s more quantum than is usually thought,” he says.
“The value of this study is that it collects a lot of information from different sources and says: ‘Look, now we see definitely that these quantum mechanical effects, these small effects due to quantum interference, are present in physical processes’,” says Vladimir Braun at the University of Regensburg in Germany.
This is the first time that an analysis of this scale has been completed and it ought to motivate further experiments, says Braun. For example, future experiments at facilities such as the Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility in Virginia could find further signatures of quantum interference and connect them to other effects that happen in fast particle collisions.
Although he never doubted the proton’s quantumness, Braun was still surprised by the details of the interference effects seen most clearly in the new work. “I was working on this kind of physics for 40 years, and I expected that the big effects will be in different place,” he says.
Going forward, the team wants to expand its dataset and analysis, and further increase the certainty of its findings. There is also the big question of how to interpret the findings and tell a more complete story of just what the proton’s insides are actually like. For example, the interference effect is related to quarks and gluons’ quantum mechanical spin, which has so far not been understood or measured very precisely.
Physicists have also yet to resolve how interference connects to forces that act on quarks and gluons, says Vladimirov. Notably, the strong nuclear force that binds quarks together is one of the four fundamental forces of nature, so understanding this would give us a better grasp of the most basic laws of our universe.

India vs Afghanistan T20I series dates confirmed; Direct clash leaves Bangladesh tour facing near-certain cancellation
Afghanistan confirmed three T20Is against India in Delhi from September 13, leaving the proposed Bangladesh tour facing cancellation due to direct date clash.
The Afghanistan Cricket Board has confirmed the dates and venue for its three-match T20I series against India, a development that has made India’s proposed white-ball tour of Bangladesh increasingly unlikely to proceed. Afghanistan will officially host India for the first time in a bilateral series, although all three matches will be staged at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi. The T20Is have been scheduled for September 13, 15 and 17.
The ACB communicated the schedule to its commercial partners through a letter sent on Monday, August 10. The board said the dates had been discussed and agreed upon with the Board of Control for Cricket in India, even though a public announcement from the relevant authorities remains pending.
“The ACB hereby confirms that the India tour of Afghanistan 2026 (Event) is scheduled to take place from September 13 to September 17. The ACB further confirms that the dates of the Event have been confirmed and agreed with the BCCI and the venues of the scheduled matches have also been finalised,” ACB CEO Naseeb Khan wrote in the letter accessed by Cricbuzz. The formal confirmation carries wider consequences for India’s international calendar because the opening Afghanistan T20I clashes directly with the final match of the proposed Bangladesh tour.
Bangladesh tour becomes virtually impossible
India had been scheduled to arrive in Bangladesh on August 28 for three ODIs and three T20Is. The ODI matches were earmarked for September 1, 3 and 6, followed by the T20Is on September 9, 12 and 13. The third Bangladesh T20I and the opening Afghanistan T20I are therefore both scheduled for September 13. Even without the direct clash, playing in Bangladesh on September 12 or 13 before beginning another international series in Delhi would leave India with an impractical travel and recovery schedule.
Unless the Bangladesh itinerary is substantially rearranged, shortened or postponed, the tour is unlikely to take place. A last-minute intervention from the two governments remains theoretically possible, but the ACB’s declaration that its dates have been agreed with the BCCI indicates that the Afghanistan series has now been given precedence.
The ACB also informed broadcasters and commercial partners that they could begin preparing for the series. “While an official public announcement regarding the event is yet to be made by the concerned authorities, the ACB is issuing this letter as an official confirmation of the scheduled dates and venues of the India tour of Afghanistan 2026. Accordingly all media rights holders may proceed with their advance planning, scheduling and production arrangements, resource allocation, promotional activities and other related preparations based on the above schedule,” the board stated.

ITW Universe, which owns the media rights, is holding discussions with JioStar, Sony Sports and Zee Unite8 over the linear broadcast rights. FanCode holds the digital rights. The ACB has also approached the BCCI about moving either the first or second match to September 14, coinciding with Ganesh Chaturthi. However, such a one-day adjustment would still not make the Bangladesh tour feasible under its present schedule.
“I would not like to comment prematurely on any potential date adjustments that the Afghanistan Cricket Board may be considering. Should such a development materialise, aligning this historic series with Ganesh Chaturthi — a day of new beginnings, devotion and celebration across India — would be a thoughtful and gracious gesture from the ACB, reflecting the spirit of friendship that cricket continues to foster between India and Afghanistan,” ITW co-founder Bhairav Shanth said.
Shanth described the series as an important moment for Afghanistan cricket. “This marks a landmark moment — Afghanistan officially hosting India in a bilateral series for the first time. ITW Universe, together with our world-class partners, will be producing the broadcast and bringing several visual and storytelling upgrades that fans have never experienced before.”

Spotify will begin labeling AI-generated artists with “AI Persona” profile tags and ban their music from its editorial and algorithmic recommendations, the company announced on Tuesday.

While Spotify will allow artists to identify themselves as AI Personas, the company says it won’t rely on self-disclosure alone.

THIS MEANS MORE (MONEY)
Far be it for Football Daily to make cheap gags [wait, what? – Football Daily Ed] relating to the involvement of Amazon founder and master of the universe Jeff Bezos in a consortium buying around 30% of Liverpool FC. Will new signings arrive via prompt delivery but end up next door at Everton? How will fans rate the packaging? Etc, etc. There’s also the involvement of Eduardo Saverin, the Facebook co-founder poking his head in. Though long ago unfriended by Mark Zuckerberg, Saverin still ranked No 56 on Forbes’s billionaires list. These are seriously rich men, and among the planet’s chino class, to quote Vladimir Putin, “soccer is popular”. The Geopolitics World Cup posh seats were full of those eyeing up deals on a frontier hardly new to investors from the USA USA USA, but where there may be much more gold to strike. See Gianni Infantino’s misreading of the art of the deal as an, ahem, prime example.
Bezos is no football man, barely known as a sports fan. Links with buying the Seattle Seahawks, his local NFL franchise, were speculative. He is, though, the third richest man in the world, according to appendage-measuring listicles. Amazon’s market value is higher than Brazil’s annual GDP. For certain people, that triggers arousal at the thought of their team being able to buy the biggest and best players in the world. Just imagine if their club was to spend, say, £446m in a single summer. How good would that be?
For others, there is a regrettable mission creep towards a civic institution – one that, despite global fame, cleaves to its local community – being tossed around by venture capitalists. Though that process has been in train since Tom Hicks and George Gillett arrived on Merseyside, full of huckster charm, almost two decades ago. The socialism and collectivism Bill Shankly envisaged for the club he made famous disappeared in the sepia-tinged rearview mirror. Football was a business even back in Shanks’ day but now attracts the richest suits of all; if Bezos is chancing his arm in football, what price Elon Musk or Google tycoon Larry Page are seen wearing the scarf of their chosen club? Oh joy.
Current overlords Fenway Sports Group, who picked up the pieces from impending disaster in 2010, are, yes, a consortium of American venture capitalists. Their existential aim is to make as much loot as possible from an asset purchased for a knockdown price of £300m. It’s gone well. This mooted deal includes Bezos, Saverin and Amit Bhatia, a frontman you may recognise from when QPR fans celebrated their owners being richer than Roman Abramovich. That did not go well. The latest deal would value the club at £4.4bn. High-fives all round, though the doubles and trebles may take time. Liverpool enter the season with an imbalanced squad, unsuited to a manager whose arrival was generally seen as a Good Thing. If football is all about money, even the biggest money cannot solve every problem.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“After careful consideration, we don’t feel it is right to proceed at this time without the necessary preparation in place, but we will remain in conversation with the club and see what is possible in the future” – one wealthy benefactor not entering the game – yet – is Turki Alalshikh, whose bid to buy a controlling interest in Derby will no longer proceed, with the club now off the market.
